passages.text:
Simon said, “Therefore, if God is the cause only of good things, what remains to be thought except that some other first principle begot evil, or that it is perhaps unbegotten?”

Peter said, “Neither did some other power beget the evil one, nor is evil unbegotten, as I shall show at the end. For my present task is to demonstrate—as I promised at the beginning—that God is blameless in every respect. We have therefore granted that God possesses, beyond comparison, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings. Consequently, he may also be the one who puts forth the four substances—I mean hot and cold, wet and dry. These, being primary, simple, and unmixed, have an inclination toward neither side; but once put forth by God and blended outside him, they may become a living being possessing the purpose of destroying evil people. And so, since all things have been generated from him, the evil one neither comes from elsewhere nor has received his wickedness from God himself, who made everything and with whom it is impossible for wickedness to exist. For the substances, being neutral, were carefully distinguished and put forth from him; and when outside him they had been blended with one another by his skill, the desire for the destruction of evil people arose by an act of will. But the resulting wickedness cannot destroy good people, not even if it should wish to, for by law it has authority against those who sin. Thus, not knowing each person’s character, the evil one gains experience by putting them to the test and, after thoroughly examining them, punishes them.”

Simon said, “Therefore, since God has the power to mix the elements and to make mixtures for whatever ends he wishes, so that whatever purposes he wishes may arise, why did he not make each person’s mixture disposed to choose good things?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ πονηρὸν ἑτέρα τις ἐγέννησεν ἀρχὴ ἢ ἄρ’ ἀγέννητόν ἐστιν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: some other first principle begot evil, or that it is perhaps unbegotten?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Simon uses the neuter τὸ πονηρόν and a neuter predicate, so “evil” and “it” preserve the wording. The personal interpretation “the evil one” is contextually possible, but Peter’s reply then observably shifts first to masculine τὸν πονηρόν and afterward back to neuter τὸ κακόν.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὔτε ἑτέρα τις δύναμις ἐγέννησεν τὸν πονηρὸν οὔτε ἀγέννητόν ἐστιν τὸ κακόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Neither did some other power beget the evil one, nor is evil unbegotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves Peter’s transition from the masculine personal expression τὸν πονηρόν to the neuter abstraction τὸ κακόν.
ἀρχή may denote a beginning, origin, source, or ruling first principle. “First principle” fits the proposed independent origin of evil, though “some other origin” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be the one who puts forth the four substances
lexical_decisions.rationale: προβολεύς describes one who projects or puts something forth. The rendering preserves the emanative image without importing a later technical system.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have an inclination toward neither side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two opposed sides are left implicit in οὐδέτερον, contextually good and evil; the translation likewise leaves them unnamed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προβληθέντα δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ [κ]αὶ ἔξω κραθέντα γενέσθαι ζῷον
lexical_decisions.chosen: once put forth by God and blended outside him, they may become a living being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive γενέσθαι can remain under the force of ἐνδέχεται from the preceding clause. The plural substances become one singular living being through blending; “they became” is also possible if the infinitive is understood more assertorically.
The rare form conveys deliberate discrimination or separation. “Carefully selected” or “carefully separated” are viable alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν κακίαν εἴληφεν ... ἡ συμβεβηκυῖα κακία
lexical_decisions.chosen: has received his wickedness ... the resulting wickedness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Rendering both occurrences of κακία as “wickedness” preserves the repeated source term and distinguishes it from τὸ κακόν, rendered “evil.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ πρὸς τὸν τῶν κακῶν ὄλεθρον ἐπιθυμία
lexical_decisions.chosen: the desire for the destruction of evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: τῶν κακῶν may denote evil people or evil things. The personal sense is favored by the preceding κακούς and the subsequent contrast with ἀγαθούς.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gains experience by putting them to the test
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ αὐτῶν presents the experience as gained through action directed against them and repeats the adversarial force of the preceding κατὰ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων. More formally, the phrase could be rendered “gains experience against them,” but that is less intelligible in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after thoroughly examining them, punishes them
lexical_decisions.rationale: διελέγχω can mean examine, expose, refute, or prove guilty. “Thoroughly examining” fits the preceding statement that the evil one initially does not know each person’s character.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποιεῖν κράσει[ς] πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make mixtures for whatever ends he wishes, so that whatever purposes he wishes may arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated relatives and shift from neuter ἃ to feminine ἃς leave the attachment compressed. The rendering relates the first phrase to intended ends and the second to προαιρέσεις; alternatively, feminine ἃς may refer directly back to κράσεις.
προαιρετικός with the genitive describes an inclination or capacity to choose the specified objects.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period after the article. It has no intelligible function as a sentence boundary here and is treated provisionally as an anomalous typographic or editorial punctuation feature, not as unverified text.
